Adult Western king wrasse, Coris auricularis, attain a maximum recorded total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a size that places them among the moderately large members of the Labridae along the temperate Australian coastline. Field surveys conducted across multiple reef habitats indicate that individuals grow rapidly during their first few years, with the asymptotic length being reached well before the onset of senescence. This ultimate size is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 809 grams [Wwi = 809 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions based on a substantial sample of mature specimens. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a typical allometric trajectory for benthic predatory fishes, with the exponent indicating positive allometric growth. Such a body plan is well-suited for the energetic demands of diurnal foraging among rocky crevices and seagrass beds, where the wrasse pursues a diet dominated by benthic invertebrates including molluscs and crustaceans. The substantial adult mass of 809 grams [Wwi = 809 grams] also reflects the capacity for storing energy reserves that support both routine metabolism and the elevated costs of reproductive activity during the spawning season.

Puberty in Western king wrasse is attained when individuals reach a total length of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 96.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 96.4 grams] based on the species-specific length-mass relationship. This size threshold appears to be a reliable indicator of gonadal maturation, as histological examination of ovarian and testicular tissue from individuals collected across a range of sizes confirms the onset of gametogenesis at this length. The timing of puberty is ecologically significant, as it represents the point at which individuals begin to allocate resources toward reproductive effort rather than solely toward somatic growth. Comparative data from other labrid species of similar body plan suggest that this length at puberty is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes reaching a relatively secure body size before investing in offspring production. The transition from the immature to the mature state is accompanied by notable changes in coloration and behaviour, with males developing the striking blue and green patterning that characterizes the adult phase.

The maximum reproductive rate of Coris auricularis has been estimated from fecundity data collected during the peak spawning period at a water temperature of 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females release on average 156,250 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 156,250 eggs per spawning event], completing a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year]. This daily production translates to approximately 438 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 438 eggs per day], reflecting the substantial energetic investment females channel into gametogenesis during the reproductive window. The spawning season extends over several months during the austral spring and summer, with individual females capable of a single, highly fecund spawning event within a season. This iteroparous strategy is typical of many temperate labrids and allows the species to buffer against interannual variability in environmental conditions that may affect larval survival. The high fecundity per event ensures that even modest survival rates among the pelagic larvae can sustain population recruitment.

Eggs of Western king wrasse are remarkably small at the moment of oviposition, with the wet weight at birth measured at 0.00039 grams [Wwb = 0.00039 grams], a value consistent with the pelagic egg diameter typical of the Labridae. This minute initial mass reflects the relatively low maternal investment per offspring, a common feature among marine fishes that produce large numbers of small, free-floating eggs. Once released into the water column, the fertilised ova undergo rapid cleavage and develop into yolk-sac larvae within a few days, with the duration of the egg stage strongly influenced by ambient temperature. The small size of the hatchling imposes a brief window for first exogenous feeding, as the endogenous yolk reserves are limited. Field observations suggest that successful transition to the planktonic larval stage depends critically on the timing of spawning relative to local peaks in microzooplankton abundance, a coupling that is particularly tight for species with such modest per-offspring provisioning. The larval period itself is characterised by high mortality rates, a life-history stage where the minute starting mass becomes a major demographic bottleneck.

Longevity in Coris auricularis has been assessed through mark-recapture studies and otolith-based ageing techniques conducted at a water temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. Under these environmental conditions, the maximum observed lifespan is 4,015 days [am = 4,015 days], which corresponds to approximately 11 years of life at a temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. This comparatively long lifespan is notable among inshore labrids of equivalent body size and likely reflects a combination of low natural predation pressure in structurally complex reef habitats and the species' relatively slow pace of life after maturity. The otolith annuli show clear annual increments that are easily interpretable, allowing confident age assignment for the oldest individuals in the sampled population. Such longevity has important implications for population dynamics, as it permits multiple years of reproductive contribution from each mature female, thereby buffering the population against occasional recruitment failures. The observed lifespan, when considered alongside the age at puberty and the annual reproductive output, places C. auricularis firmly within the slow end of the fast-slow continuum for temperate labrid fishes, a position that renders the species potentially vulnerable to overexploitation if adult mortality rates increase substantially.
